d: Of communal life sequestered from the world under religious vows
r: Medieval Latin conventuālis, from Latin conventus “convent”
s: The Breton Club resumed its meetings in the refectory of an empty conventual building in the rue Saint-Jacques.
old_f: Of formal meetings held under the rules of a governing body
Of ordinary habits followed without question by most people
Of goods shipped together under the protection of armed escort
ety: From Medieval Latin conventuālis, from Latin conventus (“convent”).

d: A remarkable or excellent thing or person
r: Cork + -er
s: He had just had an absolute corker of an idea!
old_f: A worker who seals barrels and bottles
A thick-soled shoe for wet ground
A small fish of rocky coasts
ety: From cork + -er.

d: Showing a brooding ill humor
r: Latin mōrōsus “particular, fastidious, peevish”, from mōs “way, custom, habit”
s: A morose and unsociable manner.
old_f: Showing a dark red color
Speaking slowly and with care
Covered in a thin layer of moss
ety: From French morose, from Latin mōrōsus (“particular, scrupulous, fastidious, self-willed, wayward, capricious, fretful, peevish”), from mōs (“way, custom, habit, self-will”). See moral.

d: Warning of future misfortune
r: Latin praemonitōrius
s: Many conditions formerly thought to be purely functional are now known as premonitory evidences of organic disease.
old_f: Coming before the main course
Giving advance payment
Relating to the first ministers
ety: Borrowed from Latin praemonitōrius.

d: An unexpected and inexplicable change in something (in a situation or a person’s behavior, etc.)
r: Italian vagare “wander”, from Latin vagārī “to wander”
s: Still a vagary of youth, it was held, but romantically respectable.
old_f: A formal and binding agreement between two parties (in a trade or a marriage, etc.)
A sharp and painful swelling in some part of the body (in a joint or a gland, etc.)
A small and decorative container for something (in a church or a palace, etc.)
ety: From Italian vagare (“wander”) and/or its source Latin vagārī (“to wander”), from Latin vagus (“wandering”). Later apparently reinterpreted in English as vague + -ery but without changing the spelling. By surface analysis, Latin vag(us) + -ary.

d: The collection and study of money (and coins in particular)
r: Late Latin numisma “coin”, from Greek nómisma “current coin, custom”
s: Mr. Joolby, the eminent authority on Greek numismatics?
old_f: The collection and study of insects (and moths in particular)
The collection and study of names (and surnames in particular)
The collection and study of maps (and sea charts in particular)
ety: From French numismatique, from Late Latin numisma, numismatis (“coin”), variant of Latin nomisma, from Ancient Greek νόμισμα (nómisma, “current coin, custom”), from νομίζω (nomízō, “to hold or own as a custom, usage, to use customarily, practise, to be used to”), from νόμος (nómos, “usage, custom”), from νέμω (némō, “to keep, hold, watch”).

d: A quiet song intended to lull a child to sleep
r: French berceuse
s: The engines thundered their ineffectual berceuse.
old_f: A short dance intended to open a royal ball
A wooden cradle intended for use on board ship
A light shawl intended to be worn at evening prayers
ety: Borrowed from French berceuse.

d: (used of arms and legs) bent outward with the joint away from the body
r: Middle English in kenebowe “in a sharp bend”
s: Men preferred one pose above all others, namely, the elbow akimbo.
old_f: (used of hair and beards) tangled and matted from long neglect or sleep
(used of eyes and glances) turned sideways with suspicion or distrust
(used of hats and caps) tilted back to show the wearer’s forehead
ety: From Middle English in kenebowe, in kene bowe (“in a keen bow”, i.e. “in a sharp bend or angle”), from in (“in”) + keen, kene (“brave, keen, sharp”) + bowe (“bow, bend”). Alternately, possibly from Old Norse kengr (“bent”) + bogi (“a bow”), compare Icelandic kengboginn (“bow-bent”).

d: A false accusation of an offense or a malicious misrepresentation of someone’s words or actions
r: Latin calumnia “false statement, misrepresentation”
s: Accusations of abuse were pure extortive calumny in a malicious bid to make money.
old_f: A tall stone column or a carved pillar supporting the roof of a temple or palace
A gentle calming draught or a soothing drink given to the sick before sleep
A narrow mountain pass or a steep valley used by travellers crossing the Alps
ety: From Late Middle English calumnīe (“false accusation, slander; (law) objection raised in bad faith”), borrowed from Old French calomnie (“slander, calumny”) (modern French calomnie), or directly from its etymon Latin calumnia (“false statement, misrepresentation; false accusation, malicious charge”), perhaps also related to calvor (“to deceive”). The English word is a doublet of challenge. The verb is derived from French calomnier (“to slander”), from Late Latin calumniāre, from Latin calumpniārī, calumniārī (“to blame unjustly, misrepresent, calumniate; (law) to accuse falsely, bring false in

d: A state of deterioration due to old age or long use
r: Latin dēcrepitūdō
s: He had been struck by Mao's decrepitude and Chou's failing health.
old_f: A state of complete silence due to grief or shock
A sharp crackling noise made by salt when heated
A formal reduction of rank due to misconduct
ety: From Middle French décrépitude, from Old French, from Latin dēcrepitūdō (“decrepitude”).

d: One praying humbly for something
r: French suppliant, present participle of supplier; a doublet of supplicant
s: I touch your beard as a suppliant, embrace your knees, imploring you to have pity on my wretchedness.
old_f: One who provides food to soldiers
One who is flexible and easily bent
One who replaces another in office
ety: From French suppliant, present participle of supplier. Doublet of supplicant.

d: Devoid of intelligence
r: Latin fatuus “foolish, silly, simple”
s: Don't be fatuous, Jeffrey.
old_f: Plump and well fed
Fixed by destiny
Tired and weary
ety: From Latin fatuus (“foolish, silly, simple”).

d: Large heavy rope for nautical use
r: Anglo-Norman haucer, from Vulgar Latin *altiāre “to raise”
s: A hatchet to my hawser? all adrift to go?
old_f: Small hooded falcon for hunting
Wooden peg for hanging nets
Narrow gangway for loading cargo
ety: From Middle English hauser, haucer, from Anglo-Norman haucer, from Vulgar Latin *altiāre (“to raise”), derived from Latin altus (“high”). Altered in English by mistaken association with hawse and perhaps haul. Compare French aussière, haussière.

d: Power to influence or coerce
r: Old French puissant “powerful”
s: We easily pronounce puissance, truth and justice.
old_f: A thick soup of dried peas
A small leather purse
A brief pause between notes
ety: From Middle English puissaunce, from Anglo-Norman puissance, pusaunce, and other forms, from Old French puissant (“powerful”).

d: Overbearing pride evidenced by a superior manner toward inferiors
r: French hauteur
s: Sometimes the hauteur is nothing more dire than a kind of black-mother wit.
old_f: A deep red wine produced in the valleys of eastern France
A long, flowing gown worn by women at royal courts
A rich sauce made with butter, cream and wine for game
ety: Borrowed from French hauteur.

d: An officer of the church who is in charge of sacred objects
r: Late Latin sacrista, from Latin sacer; a doublet of sexton
s: The church was looked after by an old sacristan who lived in a cottage on the shore of the lake.
old_f: A monk of the church who is in charge of the kitchen gardens
A singer in the church who leads the chanting of the psalms
A guard of the church who is in charge of the bell tower
ety: From French sacristain, Late Latin sacrista, from Latin sacer. Doublet of sexton.

d: The belief in magical spells that harness occult forces or evil spirits to produce unnatural effects in the world
r: Greek nekromanteía, from nekrós “dead” + manteía “divination”
s: That necromancy is the touch-stone of occultism.
old_f: The practice of collecting old swords, helmets and armor from battlefields to sell to wealthy collectors and museums
The study of romantic poetry written about death and grief during the early years of the nineteenth century
The craft of preserving the bodies of the dead with resins and spices for burial in elaborate tombs
ety: Circa 1300, from Middle English nigromancye, from Old French nigromancie, from Medieval Latin nigromantia, from Latin necromantia, from Ancient Greek νεκρομαντεία (nekromanteía), νεκρός (nekrós, “dead”) + μαντεία (manteía, “divination”). Medieval Latin spelling, incorporating niger (“black”), influenced by the notion of black art. Modern spelling adopted in mid-1500s. By surface analysis, necro- + -mancy.

d: Excluded from use or mention
r: German verboten “banned, forbidden”; a doublet of forbidden
s: The next day we were off-limits to one another—verboten, traife, dangerous.
old_f: Spoken aloud word for word
Covered with green growth
Twisted into a spiral
ety: Unadapted borrowing from German verboten (“banned, forbidden, prohibited”). Doublet of forbidden.

d: Temporary cessation or suspension
r: Anglo-Norman abeiance “legal expectation”, from Old French abeër “to gape at, aspire after”
s: Without a plausible explanation for what might have provoked an ice age, the whole theory fell into abeyance.
old_f: Strict obedience to rules
A small private chapel
A sudden loud cry
ety: First attested in 1528. From Anglo-Norman abeiance (“legal expectation”), from Old French abeance (“desire”) from abeër (“to gape at, aspire after”), abaer, abair (“to desire”), from a (“to”) + baër (“to gape”), bair (“yawn”), from Medieval Latin batō (“to yawn”).

d: A strong north wind that blows in France during the winter
r: Middle French mistral, from Occitan; a doublet of magistral
s: The mistral had been blowing for three days now and the sea showed more white than blue.
old_f: A wandering singer who performed at the courts of southern France
A thin sweet wine made from grapes dried in the winter sun
A heavy wooden shutter used to keep out storms in coastal villages
ety: Borrowed from Middle French mistral, from Occitan. Doublet of magistral.

d: The slender spear of the Bantu-speaking people of Africa
r: Arabic az-zaḡāya, from Proto-Berber *zaġāya “spear”
s: A collection of spears, assegais, shields, knives was hung up in trophies.
old_f: The woven grass mat used for sleeping in parts of East Africa
The beaded headband worn at weddings in parts of southern Africa
The carved wooden stool of a village elder in West Africa
ety: From French azagaie (now zagaie) or Portuguese azagaia, Spanish azagaya, and later in the forms that have become most common borrowed from Afrikaans assegaai, from colloquial Arabic اَلزَّغَايَة (az-zaḡāya), from Proto-Berber *zaġāya (“spear”).

d: Prevent the occurrence of; prevent from happening
r: Middle English forfenden “to ward off, protect, prohibit”: for- + fend
s: People have long given thought to the causes of danger and how they might be forfended.
old_f: Give up a right; lose through neglect
Predict a future event; foretell
Pardon an offense; forgive
ety: From Middle English forfenden (“to ward off, protect, prohibit”), equivalent to for- + fend.

d: A ceramic or mural decoration made by scratching off a surface layer to reveal the ground
r: Italian sgraffito, from s- “out” + graffito, ultimately from Greek gráphein “to write or scratch”
s: I did murals there as well, designs for windows, bas relief and otherwise, sgraffitoes.
old_f: A quick sketch made in charcoal or chalk on a wall to plan the layout of a fresco
A glossy glaze made by mixing ground glass with lead to coat earthenware before firing
A carved frame made of gilded wood or plaster to surround a painting in a church
ety: Borrowed from Italian sgraffito, from s- (“out”) + graffito (past participle of graffire), ultimately from Ancient Greek γράφειν (gráphein, “to write or scratch”).

d: A hussar’s jacket worn over the shoulders
r: French doliman, ultimately from Ottoman Turkish dolaman “robe”, from dolamak “to wrap around”
s: He shrugged a shoulder until his dolman fell into place.
old_f: A Turkish stuffed vine leaf served cold
A wide-brimmed hat worn by shepherds
A small hanging lamp of brass
ety: Apparently from French doliman, dolman (sense 2), ultimately from Ottoman Turkish طولامان, دولامان (dolaman, “robe”), from طولامق (dolamak, “to wrap around”). Compare German Doliman, Dollman; Hungarian dolmány.

d: Impossible to avoid or evade
r: Latin inēlūctābilis, from in- + ēlūctor “struggle out”
s: They have come under the yoke of ineluctable slavery.
old_f: Impossible to read or decipher
Impossible to put into words
Impossible to wash clean
ety: From Middle French inéluctable (whence in- + e- and -able), from Latin inēlūctābilis, from in- + ēlūctor (“struggle out”) + -bilis.

d: Talk socially without exchanging too much information
r: Northern English dialect gnatter “to chatter, grumble”, ultimately imitative
s: What are you guys nattering about? You're clearly not following the meeting!
old_f: Tie knots in a fishing net
Groom one’s hair with oil
Sneeze repeatedly from dust
ety: From a Northern England dialectal variant of gnatter (also knatter) ("to chatter, grumble; nibble away at"), ultimately of imitative origin. Cognate with German Low German gnattern (“to mumble, grumble, be grouchy”).

d: A person who drinks alcohol to excess habitually
r: Dipso- + -maniac
s: The dipsomaniac and the abstainer are not only both mistaken, but they both make the same mistake.
old_f: A person who bathes in cold water every morning
A person who swims or dives at great depths without equipment
A person who collects rare stamps and coins compulsively
ety: From dipso- + -maniac.

d: Requiring secret or mysterious knowledge
r: Latin arcānus “hidden, secret”, from arceō “to shut up, enclose”
s: He had an arcane knowledge of ancient rituals.
old_f: Curved like a bow
Very old and outdated
Fond of bright colors
ety: Borrowed from Latin arcānus (“hidden, secret”), from arceō (“to shut up, enclose”); cognate with Latin arca (“a chest”).

d: Tending to promote physical well-being; beneficial to health
r: Latin salutaris “healthful”, from salus “health”
s: Groper argues that “being digital” is constitutive of today’s salutary political life.
old_f: Tending to welcome guests warmly; offering a friendly greeting
Containing a high level of salt; briny to the taste
Relating to wages and salaries; paid at regular intervals
ety: Borrowed from Middle French salutaire and its source, Latin salutaris (“healthful”), from salus (“health”).

d: Thick cushion used as a seat
r: Old English hassoc “coarse grass”, of uncertain origin
s: At the next service he found a flower on his hassock.
old_f: Tall boot worn by riders
Coarse sack for grain
Short cloak with a hood
ety: From Old English hassoc (“coarse grass”), of uncertain origin.

d: Dull and tiresome but with pretensions of significance or originality
r: Platitude + -ous
s: Situations and emotions that would remain exasperatingly vague to the reader had their expression been etiolated by means of platitudinous evasions.
old_f: Broad and flat but with a slight upward curve at each end
Plump and rounded but with a firm and healthy appearance
Pale and shiny but with a faint silvery tint
ety: From platitude + -ous on analogy of other adjectives ending in -tudinous, from Latin -tūdin- + -ous, the oblique stem of -tūdō. Compare platitudinize.

d: A crafty and involved plot to achieve your (usually sinister) ends
r: Latin māchinātiōnem, from māchinor “devise, invent”
s: The inner machinations of my mind are an enigma.
old_f: A loud and repeated noise made by a machine (usually a loom)
A careful and gradual process of shaping metal (usually by hand)
A large and complicated device for lifting heavy loads (usually in docks)
ety: From Middle English machynacion, machynacyon, from Middle French machination and directly Latin māchinātiōnem, from māchinor (“devise, invent”). By surface analysis, machinate + -ion or machine + -ation.

d: Total certainty or greater certainty than circumstances warrant
r: Late Latin certitūdō, from Latin certus
s: Taxes are obviously certitudes.
old_f: A formal document stating the holder’s qualifications
A narrow mountain pass or gorge
A measure of land equal to one acre
ety: From Middle French certitude, from Late Latin certitūdō, from Latin certus.

d: Offer as a sacrifice by killing or by giving up to destruction
r: Latin immolō “to sacrifice”
s: The Aztecs immolated human victims.
old_f: Protect from harm by sealing inside a coat of wax or resin
Make softer by soaking in water or giving up to warmth
Hold perfectly still by binding tightly or giving up to restraint
ety: The adjective is first attested in 1534, the verb in 1548; borrowed from Latin immolātus, perfect passive participle of immolō (“to sacrifice”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

d: Dedicated in fulfillment of a vow
r: Latin vōtīvus, from vōtum “vow”
s: She placed a votive offering at the shrine.
old_f: Relating to the casting of ballots
Spoken aloud in a loud voice
Moving in a spiral or whirl
ety: From Middle French votif, from Latin vōtīvus (“votive”), from vōtum (“vow”).

d: Ostentatiously lofty in style
r: Declaim + -atory
s: Behind him an excitable Frenchman was holding forth in declamatory style to a group of astonished residents.
old_f: Sloping gently downward
Openly stated or announced
Lacking any clear meaning
ety: Equivalent to declaim + -atory.

d: A concise reference book providing specific information about a subject or location
r: Greek enkheirídion “handbook, manual”, from en “in” + kheír “hand”
s: Sartor Resartus was for many years his Enchiridion (he says).
old_f: A long epic poem recounting the adventures of a legendary hero or founder
A small jeweled case used for carrying perfume or relics on a chain
A spell or charm recited to protect a household from evil spirits
ety: Either via Latin enchīridion or directly, from Ancient Greek ἐγχειρίδιον (enkheirídion, “handbook, manual”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + χείρ (kheír, “hand”) + -ίδιον (-ídion).

d: In good time
r: Middle English betymes, from bi “by” + time + adverbial -s
s: Smart lad to slip betimes away From fields where glory does not stay.
old_f: From time to time
At bedtime
Between meals
ety: From Middle English betymes, from bi (“by”) + time + adverbial -s. By surface analysis, betime + -s (adverbial suffix). Compare also betides.

d: Traffic in ecclesiastical offices or preferments
r: Late Latin simonia, after Simon Magus (Acts 8:18–20)
s: He openly practiced simony; in other words, he sold benefices.
old_f: Imitation of another’s speech or manners
Harmony of many voices singing together
Likeness between two unrelated things
ety: From Middle English simonie, symonye, from Old French simonie, from Late Latin simonia, named after Simon Magus (Hebrew שִׁמְעוֹן (Šimʻôn, “Simon”)), with reference to Acts 8:18–20.

d: A sleeveless cape that is lined or trimmed with fur
r: French pelisse, from Latin pellis “skin”; a doublet of pilch
s: The mother was crimson in countenance and pelisse.
old_f: A small round tablet of compressed herbs
A shallow wooden spade used for removing bread from an oven
A thin wafer of dough baked with sugar
ety: Borrowed from French pelisse, from Late Latin pellicia, from Latin pellis (“skin”). Doublet of pilch.
